senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior

reason or cause for an event or state
reason or cause for an event or state

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior

senses.comment: In a number of languages it may be difficult to employ a highly abstract term such as ‘truth.’ Accordingly, one may find it necessary to relate ‘truth’ in Galatians 4:16 to the immediate context, for example, ‘… by telling you what they really want to do’ or ‘… what all this really means.’

senses.def: that which is given as a means of recompense or repayment
senses.comment: One may also translate ‘repayment to their parents and grandparents’ as ‘to pay back to their parents and grandparents for what these have done for them’ or ‘to help their parents and grandparents because of what these have done to help them.’

senses.domain: Stances and Events Related to Stances
senses.def: to cause someone to lie down

senses.domain: Stances and Events Related to Stances
senses.def: to cause someone to assume a reclining (or possibly sitting) position as part of the process of eating

senses.domain: Stances and Events Related to Stances

pertaining to that which cannot be fully related or communicated
a statement which involves direct contradiction or is logically inconsistent
shining, either in the sense of radiance from a source or the reflection of a source of light
senses.comment: It is impossible to determine whether ἀπαύγασμα should be interpreted in an active sense and therefore ‘radiance,’ or in a passive sence and therefore as ‘reflection.’ If the meaning is ‘radiance,’ then one may translate this phrase in Hebrews 1:3 as ‘he shines with God’s glory’ or even ‘God’s glory shines through him.’ If one understands the meaning of ἀπαύγασμα as being ‘reflection,’ then one may often say ‘God’s glory shines back from him.’

senses.def: to cut in such a way as to cause separation

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: a time shortly before or shortly after the time of the discourse

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: pertaining to an extremely short period of time between a previous state or event and a subsequent state or event (in a number of contexts there is the implication of unexpectedness; but this seems to be a derivative of the context as a whole and not a part of the meaning of the lexical items)

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: the present hour) an emphatic reference to a point of time which is simultaneous with another point of time
pertaining to not being able to come to some agreement
to cause (or permit) a person or persons to leave a particular location
to move away from, with the implication of resulting separation
to let something be put behind in a place
to permit something to continue in a place
to dissolve the marriage bond
senses.comment: Expressions for divorce are often based on terms meaning literally ‘to send away,’ ‘to separate from,’ or ‘to leave one another.’ However, in a number of languages idiomatic expressions are employed, for example ‘to send him off with his clothes,’ ‘to untie the knot between them,’ or ‘to throw away her hearthstones.’|Some persons have attempted to make an important distinction between ἀφίημι in 1 Corinthians 7:11 and χωρίζω in 1 Corinthians 7:15 on the assumption that ἀφίημι implies legal divorce, while χωρίζω only relates to separation. Such a distinction, however, seems to be quite artificial.

senses.def: to remove the guilt resulting from wrongdoing
senses.comment: It is extremely important to note that the focus in the meanings of ἀφίημι[f], ἄφεσις[a], and ἀπολύω[e] is upon the guilt of the wrongdoer and not upon the wrongdoing itself. The event of wrongdoing is not undone, but the guilt resulting from such an event is pardoned. To forgive, therefore, means essentially to remove the guilt resulting from wrongdoing.|Some languages make a clear distinction between guilt and sin, and terms for forgiveness are therefore related to guilt and not to the wrongdoing. Therefore, ‘to forgive sins’ is literally ‘to forgive guilt.’ Though terms for ‘forgiveness’ are often literally ‘to wipe out,’ ‘to blot out,’ or ‘to do away with,’ it is obviously not possible to blot out or to wipe out an event, but it is possible to remove or obliterate the guilt.

senses.def: to release a person from the obligation of repaying what is owed
to no longer pay attention to previous beliefs
to stop doing something, with the implication of complete cessation
to cease, of a state
to leave it to someone to do something, with the implication of distancing oneself from the event
a marker of an agent relation with numerable events, with the implication of something which proceeds from an agent
(an idiom, possibly an adage, literally: let the dead bury their dead) the matter in question is not the real issue
glosses: that is not what I mean
senses.comment: Some scholars, however, understand this expression as merely a figurative reference to various types of people and thus translate ‘let those who are spiritually dead take care of their own dead.’

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to send away the spirit) interpreted by some as implying voluntarily laying down one’s life, but such an inference is not justified by normal Greek usage)
pertaining to being of great value or worth, implying in some contexts a monetary scale
to conduct oneself, with focus upon everyday activity
a son of Jacob and ancestor of an Israelite tribe
pertaining to possessing purported good character or quality
to make known the character or significance of something by visual, auditory, gestural, or linguistic means
senses.comment: For another interpretation of δείκνυμι in 1 Corinthians 12:31, see δείκνυμι[b] 33.150.

senses.def: to explain the meaning or significance of something by demonstration
senses.comment: For another interpretation of δείκνυμι in 1 Corinthians 12:31, see δείκνυμι[a] 28.47.

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: to mark the passage of time
to cause someone to believe something that is quite different
glosses: to cause someone to turn away from a belief
senses.comment: For another interpretation of διαστρέφω in Luke 23:2, see 88.264.

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to cause someone to depart from correct behavior and thus engage in serious wrongdoing
senses.comment: For another interpretation of διαστρέφω in Luke 23:2, see 31.71. In rendering διαστρέφω as ‘to pervert,’ one should not understand the meaning in terms of ‘sexual perversion.’ In speaking of ‘perverting our people’ in Luke 23:2, it would be better in most languages to translate ‘to cause our people to go astray’ or ‘to cause them to do what they certainly should not do.’

senses.def: to cause a state to cease by a diversion to some other state, usually with the implication of a wrong state
the result of having corrected a wrong or bad situation
senses.comment: In some languages ‘reforms’ may be rendered as ‘changes from bad to good’ or ‘making things what they should be’ or ‘causing new good customs.’

senses.def: cardinal number, where there are two instances of a countable entity
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is not possible to use numbers as pronominal substitutes for specific references to animate or inanimate objects. Accordingly, in Matthew 8:28 one must often translate as ‘two men possessed by demons.’

senses.def: pertaining to being firmly established in one’s position or opinions
to permit the use of property or assets in exchange for remuneration
senses.comment: In some languages it may be necessary to specify quite clearly the implications of ‘renting out land,’ for example, ‘he let farmers grow crops on his land in exchange for a part of the harvest.’

senses.def: to bring an activity to a successful finish
a person in the genealogy of Jesus
(derivative of δύναμαι ‘to be able,’ 74.5) to cause someone to have the ability to do or to experience something
to become able to do something
to lead or bring out of a structure or area
to cause to move up
senses.comment: In a number of languages one cannot speak of ‘raising hands,’ since this would imply something that was detached from the body. It may therefore be necessary to say ‘extending hands upwards.’

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to raise up the head) to demonstrate courage in the face of danger or adversity
senses.comment: A literal rendering of ἐπαίρω τὴν κεφαλήν ‘to lift up the head’ can be misleading in some languages, since the expression may be an idiom meaning ‘to be proud’ or ‘to try to take precedence over others.’ A more satisfactory equivalent in some languages may be ‘to look up.’

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to lift one’s heel against) to oppose someone by turning against such a person, possibly with focus upon the initial aspect of becoming opposed to
senses.comment: In a number of languages a convenient way of rendering ‘to turn against’ may be ‘to become an enemy of.’

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to lift up the eyes) to direct one’s attention to something by looking closely at
(an idiom, literally: to raise the voice) to increase the volume with which one speaks, so as to overcome existing noise or the speech of someone else
(a figurative extension of meaning of ἐπαίρομαι ‘to rise up,’ not occurring in the NT) to rise up in opposition against

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to become haughty in one’s attitude toward others

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: pertaining to being gracious and forbearing
to cause someone to stop talking
a Christian from Asia Minor
to speak of something in favorable terms
excessive praise
senses.comment: In some languages flattery is expressed in a descriptive manner, for example, ‘to say that a person is wonderful when he really isn’t.’ Sometimes flattery is expressed idiomatically, for example, ‘to use big words about a small person’ or ‘to call a donkey a man.’

senses.def: to ask God to bestow divine favor on, with the implication that the verbal act itself constitutes a significant benefit
senses.comment: In a number of languages the closest equivalent of ‘to bless’ is ‘to pray God on behalf of’ or ‘to ask God to do something good for.’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (derivative of εὐλογέω[c] ‘to bless,’ 88.69) the content of the act of blessing
senses.comment: In Romans 15:29 this blessing is something which Christ has extended to Paul, in other words, a type of special favor granted to Paul by Christ.

senses.def: (derivative of εὐλογέω[b] ‘to bless,’ 33.470) that which is bestowed or given as a blessing or benefit
(an idiom, literally: on the basis of blessings) a large amount of something, with the implication of blessing or benefit
senses.comment: In translating 2 Corinthians 9:6 it may be necessary to indicate clearly the objects which form the abundance, for example, ‘the one who plants a great deal of grain will reap a very large crop.’

senses.def: to have or possess objects or property (in the technical sense of having control over the use of such objects)
to hold on to an object

senses.subdomain: Have an Opinion, Hold a View
senses.def: to hold a view or have an opinion with regard to something
to wear clothes
to possess the capacity to do something
to experience a state or condition, generally involving duration
to be in a particular state or condition

senses.subdomain: Agent in a Causative Role Marked by Verbs
senses.def: a marker of a causative relation, with otherwise almost empty semantic content
a marker of designations of content
(an idiom, literally: to have in recognition) to recognize something as being what it truly is
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ἐπίγνωσις in Romans 1:28, see 28.2.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to have in common) to share with one another equitably
senses.comment: The mutuality of sharing may be expressed in some languages as ‘each person shared with all of the rest’ or ‘each person gave to the others and received from the others.’

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to have a part in) to experience along with others
(an idiom, literally: to have ear) to be able to hear, with the implication of being expected to hear or having the obligation to hear (with a further implication of related mental activity)
senses.comment: In rendering the idiom ἔχω οὖς in Revelation 2:7, the implication is that the individuals involved ought to be able to hear and pay attention.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to have a spirit of python, an appositional construction in Greek) to tell people for pay what would happen to them in the future
(an idiom, literally: to be at an extreme) to be very sick, with the implication of imminent death
(an idiom, literally: to have badly, or: to fare badly) to be in a bad state, to be ill
glosses: to be sick (to some extent equivalent to the English idiom to be bad off in speaking of ill health)

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to have well) the state of being healthy, well (in contrast with sickness)
senses.comment: In a number of languages health is expressed only in terms of strength, for ‘to be well’ is ‘to be strong.’ In other languages, however, to be well or to be healthy is a negation of illness or sickness, so that in Mark 16:18 one may translate ‘they will place their hands on those who are sick and these people will become not sick.’

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to have bed, though in combination with ἔχω, κοίτη early acquired the metonymic meaning of sexual relations) to be in a state of pregnancy
senses.comment: This expression contrasts with the meaning of συλλαμβάνω[b], 23.49, in that it seems to focus more upon the state of pregnancy rather than the event of conception.

senses.def: (a participial form of ἔχω[a] ‘to have,’ 57.1) a position contiguous to another position
(an idiom, literally: to have in the womb) to be in a state of pregnancy
senses.comment: This expression contrasts with the meaning of συλλαμβάνω[b], 23.49, in that it seems to focus more upon the state of pregnancy rather than the event of conception.|It is impossible to determine whether in Matthew 1:23 (ἐν γαστρὶ ἕξει καὶ τέξεται υἱόν ‘she will be pregnant and bear a son’) the focus is upon the state of pregnancy or the fact of conception (see 23.49).

senses.subdomain: Units of Time with Reference to Other Units or Points of Time: Yesterday, Today, Next Day
senses.def: a day immediately following a previous day
Herod I, known as Herod the Great
Herod Antipas, son of Herod I, who had John the Baptist executed
Herod Agrippa I, grandson of Herod I
to cause oneself to become warm
senses.comment: In some languages a literal meaning of ‘to warm oneself’ would mean ‘to increase in anger,’ and therefore it may be necessary in a case such as Mark 14:67 to say simply ‘when she saw Peter there near the fire.’

senses.def: to cause someone to become well again after having been sick
senses.comment: In a number of languages there are different terms for ‘healing’ depending upon the type of sickness or illness which is involved.

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of ἰάομαι[a] ‘to heal,’ 23.136) to cause something to change to an earlier, correct, or appropriate state
an additional name of Joseph Barsabbas, one of two candidates for the place of Judas Iscariot
an additional name of Titius, a Jewish proselyte Acts 18:7)
Jesus called Justus, a companion of Paul
(derivative of καθηγέομαι ‘to guide, to explain,’ not occurring in the NT) one who provides instruction and guidance
to engage in retail business, with the implication of deceptiveness and greedy motives
to kill or attempt to kill by means of hurling stones, normally carried out by angry mobs

senses.subdomain: Regions Below the Surface of the Earth
senses.def: pertaining to being below the surface of the earth
senses.comment: In Philippians 2:10 καταχθονίων is probably a reference to the dead, generally regarded as inhabiting a dark region under the ground.

senses.def: (a diminutive derivative of κέρας[a] ‘horn,’ 8.17) the pod of the carob tree (which closely resembles a small horn)
senses.comment: Carob pods were commonly used for fattening swine and were employed as an article of food by poor people. In translating Luke 15:16 it is not necessary, however, to identify specifically carob pods. In most languages some such expression as ‘edible pods’ is probably more satisfactory, since carob trees are unlikely to be known.

senses.subdomain: Events Involving Liquids and Dry Masses
senses.def: a moving ridge or succession of swells on the surface of a body of water
to cause something to weigh less
(derivative of Κυρήνη ‘Cyrene,’ 93.512) a person who lives in or is a native of Cyrene
a tax collector and one of the twelve apostles, generally regarded as being the same as Matthew, 93.244
a son of Jacob and ancestor of an Israelite tribe
the son of Μελχί[a] in the genealogy of Jesus
the son of Συμεών[e] in the genealogy of Jesus
the means or instrument by which release or deliverance is made possible
senses.comment: ‘To liberate’ many may be expressed in many languages as ‘to cause people to go free’ or, in a more idiomatic manner, ‘to untie many’ or ‘to unchain many.’

senses.def: to provide information about a person or an event concerning which the speaker has direct knowledge
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is necessary to indicate specifically what is the content of a witness, so that, for example, in Luke 21:13 it may be necessary to say ‘this is your chance to witness to the good news’ or ‘… to tell about the good news’ or ‘… to tell what you yourselves know about the good news.’

senses.def: to speak well of a person on the basis of personal experience
senses.comment: It is possible that μαρτυρέω in Luke 4:22 should be translated as ‘they were well impressed.’

senses.def: a part in contrast with a whole
an area at the side of an object
region or regions of the earth, normally in relation to some ethnic group or geographical center, but not necessarily constituting a unit of governmental administration
glosses: district (though this might imply too precisely a governmental area)
senses.comment: The meanings of γῆ[d], χώρα[b], κλίμαὅριον, and μέρος[c] are not to be regarded as completely synonymous, but in certain of their NT usages they are largely overlapping in reference.

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: a group of people having specific membership and forming a part of a larger constituency
senses.comment: In the NT μέρος[d] occurs only in the expression μέρος τῶν Φαρισαίων the party of the Pharisees, and though the Pharisees constituted a socio-religious group, the use of μέρος[d] does not focus upon this socio-religious aspect of the Pharisees relationship to the Jewish nation as a whole, but merely upon their identity as a part of a larger constituency. The expression the party of the Pharisees may be rendered in some languages as the group to which the Pharisees belonged or those who were counted as Pharisees or the division called Pharisees. In selecting a word for party or group, it is important to avoid a term which would be essentially political in meaning. If there is no general term for party, it may be necessary to use one with a socio-religious denotation, since that would be the most accurate way of identifying the Pharisees in their relationship to other distinctive groups in the Jewish nation.

senses.def: a particular kind of business activity or occupation
a degree which is only part of some totality
(idioms, literally: from a part) the state of being part of something

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: from a part) pertaining to a relatively short period of time, with emphasis upon the temporary nature of the event or state

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time with Reference to Some Point of Time: Until, Delay, Still, From
senses.def: the negation of extending time up to and beyond an expected point
a legendary story or account, normally about supernatural beings, events, or cultural heroes, and in the NT always with an unfavorable connotation
senses.comment: The term μῦθος may often be translated simply as ‘untrue stories’ or ‘false tales.’

senses.def: a person in the genealogy of Jesus
(a borrowing based on Latin sextarius, a Roman measure equal to about a half liter, one pint) a kind of small pitcher or jar
a degree which almost equals some point on a scale of extent, but not quite
senses.comment: In a number of languages it may be difficult to render the degree ‘which falls just short of the precise extent.’ For example, in the case of 2 Peter 2:18 an equivalent of τοὺς ὀλίγως ἀποφεύγοντας (GNT4) may be ‘those who were just starting to escape.’

senses.def: an event in which something appears vividly and credibly to the mind, although not actually present, but implying the influence of some divine or supernatural power or agency
that which appears or is seen
senses.comment: ὅρασις[b] in Revelation 4:3 may be rendered in some languages as ‘as seen’ or ‘to the eyes’ or ‘to look at,’ for example, ‘and he who sat upon it was similar to a jasper stone to look at’ or ‘to look at the one who sat on it was like looking at a jasper stone.’

senses.def: space above the earth, including the vault arching high over the earth from one horizon to another, as well as the sun, moon, and stars
senses.comment: In Acts 2:5 the expression ‘under the sky’ is better translated in a number of languages as ‘on earth,’ and in Hebrews 11:12 ‘the stars of the sky’ is effectively rendered in many instances as ‘the stars up above,’ though in many languages ‘up above’ is not only redundant, but misleading, since it might suggest stars that would not be ‘up above.’ The area described by the phrase ἀπ’ ἄκρων οὐρανῶν ἕως τῶν ἄκρων αὐτῶν in Matthew 24:31 refers to the limits of the horizon regarded as the limits of the sky, but in many languages the equivalent is an expression dealing with the limits of the earth.|In some contexts οὐρανός[a] ‘sky’ designates areas which in other languages are referred to by terms specifying only a part of the area above the earth. For example, a literal translation of ἐμβλέψατε εἰς τὰ πετεινὰ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ ‘look at the birds of the sky’ (Matthew 6:26) would in some languages refer only to those birds which fly particularly high in the sky, for example, eagles, vultures, and falcons. The Greek expression τὰ πετεινὰ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ simply designates wild birds in contrast with domestic fowl, such as chickens. Therefore, in translating ‘the birds of the sky,’ one may wish to use a general designation for all wild birds. See also 4.41.|The sky (οὐρανός[a]) is also represented in the Scriptures as a dwelling place of certain supernatural beings, for the various stars and constellations were associated with supernatural forces (see στρατιὰ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ, literally ‘the army of heaven,’ in Acts 7:42: ὁ θεὸς … παρέδωκεν αὐτοὺς λατρεύειν τῇ στρατιᾷ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ ‘God … gave them over to worship the stars of the heaven’). In some languages, however, there is a problem with the rendering ‘stars of heaven,’ since such an expression might imply that there are types of stars which do not exist in the sky. Therefore, it is often more appropriate to translate στρατιὰ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ as simply ‘the stars.’ At the same time it is often advisable to introduce a marginal note to indicate that the stars were regarded as symbols of supernatural beings. One may also translate στρατιὰ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ as ‘supernatural beings in the sky’ or ‘powers that dwell in the sky’ (see 12.45).|The semantic equivalent of οὐρανός[a] is in some instances merely an adverb meaning ‘up’ or ‘above.’ In other languages the various areas referred to by ούρανός[a] must be designated by more specific terms or phrases, for example, ‘the region of the stars,’ ‘the place of the clouds,’ or ‘where the wind blows,’ as a way of designating at least three different areas which may be significant in certain types of contexts.

senses.def: the supernatural dwelling place of God and other heavenly beings (οὐρανός[b] also contains a component denoting that which is above or in the sky, but the element of abode is evidently more significant than location above the earth)
senses.comment: In a number of languages precisely the same term is used to designate both ‘sky’ and ‘heaven’ (as the abode of God). But in many instances a completely separate term must be employed in speaking of the dwelling place of God, for example, ‘where God lives’ or ‘where God is’ or ‘from where God governs.’ In some languages the term referring to ‘heaven’ is simply ‘the home above,’ and in one instance a designation of heaven refers primarily to a state, for example, ‘the life above.’|The phrase τρίτος οὐρανός ‘the third heaven’ is a fixed phrase referring to the abode of God (ἁρπαγέντα τὸν τοιοῦτον ἕως τρίτου οὐρανοῦ ‘(a man) who was caught up as far as the third heaven’ 2 Corinthians 12:2), but in a number of languages it is extremely difficult to speak of ‘the third heaven,’ especially if one uses a term for ‘heaven’ which is ‘the abode of God.’ Therefore, in many instances τρίτος οὐρανός is translated as ‘heaven’ or ‘the abode of God,’ and if necessary, a footnote may be added in order to indicate the literal meaning of the Greek expression. If a literal rendering is employed, it is usually equivalent to ‘the third sky’ or ‘above two degrees of sky.’

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of οὐρανός[b] ‘heaven,’ 1.11) a reference to God based on the Jewish tendency to avoid using a name or direct term for God
senses.comment: A translation such as ‘I have sinned against God’ would seem to be so much simpler than ‘I have sinned against heaven,’ but in reality it is not easy to find a satisfactory expression for ‘sinning against God.’ It is, of course, possible to speak of ‘fighting against a person,’ but ‘to sin against a person’ involves a very complex relationship which often needs to be more clearly explained, for example, ‘I have sinned against what God has said’ or ‘I have sinned by doing what displeases God.’ In some languages a strictly literal rendering of ‘I have sinned against God’ might be understood in the sense of committing some kind of sin with God.

senses.def: a more or less fixed phrase: the heavens and the earth, equivalent to a single lexical item: the totality of God’s creation
senses.comment: There may be certain complications involved in rendering ὁ οὐρανὸς καὶ ἡ γῆ as ‘heaven and earth,’ since ‘heaven’ might be interpreted in some languages as referring only to the dwelling place of God himself. The referents in this passage are ‘the sky and the earth,’ in other words, all of physical existence, but not the dwelling place of God, for the latter would not be included in what is destined to pass away.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: birds of the sky) wild birds in contrast with domesticated birds such as chickens
senses.comment: A literal rendering of πετεινὰ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ, either as ‘birds of the air’ or ‘birds of the sky,’ may be misleading, since ‘birds of the air’ might imply that these are birds made out of air, and ‘birds of the sky’ might suggest they are birds which remain always in the sky. In some languages the equivalent expression is ‘birds of the trees’ or ‘birds of the winds.’

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: army of heaven) the stars of heaven as symbols of various supernatural powers
senses.comment: Since ‘the stars of heaven’ serve primarily as symbols of certain heavenly supernatural powers, it may be appropriate in some languages to speak of ‘the spirits of the stars in the sky.’ See also 1.5.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: under the sky) pertaining to being on the earth
senses.comment: ὑπὸ τὸν οὐρανόν is essentially equivalent in reference to ἐπίγειος ‘on the earth’ (1.41).

senses.def: all possible positions
senses.comment: The expression πάντῃ τε καὶ πανταχοῦ in Acts 24:3 is repetitive for the sake of emphasis. Some scholars, however, interpret πάντῃ in Acts 24:3 as ‘at all times,’ in which case Acts 24:3 would be a rare example of this meaning of πάντῃ in Greek.

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time with Reference to Some Point of Time: Until, Delay, Still, From
senses.def: to extend a period of time
senses.comment: For another interpretation of παρατείνω in Acts 20:7, see 68.21.

senses.def: to cause an event to continue beyond an expected period of time
the region or population center from which a person comes, that is to say, the place of one’s birth or childhood or the place from which one’s family has come
senses.comment: In some languages a very clear distinction is made between three different references of a term such as πατρίς: (1) the place from which one’s family has come, (2) the place where one is born, and (3) the place where one normally resides. Special care, therefore, must be exercised in translating a passage such as Mark 6:1.

senses.def: to be located around some object or area
to lie or be placed around
senses.comment: In Luke 17:2 there is a problem involved in placing a millstone around a person’s neck, for millstones normally had no such hole through which a head might be placed. Therefore, it is usually necessary to translate this expression in Luke 17:2 as ‘to have a millstone hung around one’s neck’ or ‘to hang a millstone to a person’s neck.’

senses.def: to have in a position around oneself
to be in a state involving various aspects
to cause something to be completely full
to cause to happen, with the implication of fulfilling some purpose

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Duration of Time: Beginning, End
senses.def: to come to the end of a period of time, with the implication of the completion of an implied purpose or plan
senses.comment: In a number of languages it may be difficult to speak of a period of time being ‘complete.’ In Luke 1:23 one may often translate as ‘when he had finished his period of service’ or even ‘when he had done his work.’ In the case of Acts 7:30, the expression ‘after forty years were completed’ may be rendered in some languages as ‘after forty years were passed’ or ‘when forty years had happened.’

senses.def: to experience a complete degree of involvement in some event or state

senses.subdomain: Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
senses.def: a long robe reaching to the feet
glosses: a robe reaching to the feet

senses.def: a city on the coast of Italy, south of Rome
to so influence others as to cause them to follow a recommended course of action
senses.comment: In some languages it is difficult to distinguish readily between expressions for ‘leading’ and those which refer to ‘ruling’ or ‘governing,’ but it is important to try to distinguish clearly between these two different sets of interpersonal relations. In some languages, the concept of ‘leading’ can be expressed by ‘showing how to’ or ‘demonstrating how one ought to.’ In other languages it is possible to speak of ‘leading’ as simply ‘going ahead of,’ but too often such an expression may designate only ‘a scout’ who goes ahead to see whether things are safe, or it may refer only to a person who insists on his prerogative as the most distinguished person in a group.|The phrase ‘in the Lord’ in 1 Thessalonians 5:12 probably refers to matters concerning the Christian life.

senses.def: to be engaged in helping or aiding
glosses: to be involved in giving aid

senses.def: to engage in something with intense devotion
an obstacle or difficulty which may be encountered
senses.comment: For other interpretations of προσκοπή in 2 Corinthians 6:3, see 25.183 and 88.307.

senses.def: an occasion or reason for taking offense
glosses: what causes someone to be offended
senses.comment: For other interpretations of προσκοπή in 2 Corinthians 6:3, see 22.14 and 88.307.

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: that which provides an opportunity or occasion for causing someone to sin
glosses: that which causes someone to sin or that which provides an occasion for someone to sin
senses.comment: For other interpretations of προσκοπή in 2 Corinthians 6:3, see 22.14 and 25.183.

senses.def: pertaining to being a firstborn child (normally in contexts speaking of people but also used in reference to domestic animals)
senses.comment: In Jewish society the rights and responsibilities of being a firstborn son resulted in considerable prestige and status. The firstborn son, for example, received twice as much in inheritance as any other offspring.|The use of πρωτότοκος ‘firstborn’ does not imply in Greek that other children were also born to a woman, though in a number of languages one would never use ‘firstborn’ unless other children followed. Such an individual would be spoken of merely as ‘the only child.’ It is also frequently necessary to employ an appropriate qualifier for ‘firstborn’ in order to mark clearly the fact that it is ‘a firstborn son’ rather than ‘a firstborn daughter.’|The figurative meaning of πρωτότοκος in the messianic title πρωτότοκος πάσης κτίσεως ‘firstborn of all creation’ (Colossians 1:15 may be interpreted as ‘existing before all creation’ (see 13.79) or ‘existing superior to all creation’ (see 87.47).

senses.def: pertaining to existing prior to something else
senses.comment: It is possible to understand πρωτότοκος in Colossians 1:15 as ‘superior in status’ (see 87.47). See also discussion at 10.43.

senses.subdomain: High Status or Rank [including persons of high status]
senses.def: pertaining to being superior to everything else in the same or related class
senses.comment: For another interpretation of πρωτότοκος in Colossians 1:15, see 13.79; see also discussion at 10.43.

senses.def: a small, slender instrument, pointed on one end and with a hole at the other end, used in passing thread through cloth in sewing
senses.comment: There is no convincing evidence that the expression ‘eye of a needle’ in Matthew 19:24 and Luke 18:25 is a figurative name for a narrow gate. The reference to a camel passing through the eye of a needle is a case of rhetorical hyperbole, that is to say, a purposeful exaggeration to point out the extreme difficulty of the event referred to.

senses.def: (derivative of Σαμάρεια ‘Samaria,’ 93.568) a woman who is a native of Samaria
a Christian in the Jerusalem church and an associate of Paul
wine drugged with myrrh and used as a stupefying potion
senses.comment: In general, ἐσμυρνισμένος οἶνος must be rendered by means of a phrase or a clause, for example, ‘wine which has been mixed with a drug called myrrh’ or ‘wine mixed with a drug to reduce pain.’ It is, of course, also possible to use an abbreviated phrase such as ‘myrrhed wine’ and then to place the explanation of its function in a marginal note.

senses.def: one of the seven helpers in the church in Jerusalem and the first Christian martyr
(figurative extension of meaning of συγχέω or συγχύννω ‘to pour together, to mix,’ not occurring in the NT) to cause such astonishment as to bewilder and dismay
senses.comment: It is also possible to render this expression in Acts 21:27 as ‘they stirred up the whole crowd.’

senses.def: to count up or calculate a total
to be built together with some other object or objects
senses.comment: The context of Ephesians 2:22 is, of course, figurative.

senses.def: a person who sends greetings in Romans 16:21
(derivative of τελέω[e] ‘to pay taxes,’ 57.178) a place where taxes or revenue was collected from those entering a town to sell produce
senses.comment: In the ancient world taxes were primarily of two types: (1) a head tax on each individual (which was relatively small) and (2) revenue or tribute paid for goods and produce brought into an area for sale. The latter was essentially a kind of ‘sales tax,’ but paid by the seller who obviously increased the prices of goods accordingly.

senses.def: (derivative of τράπεζα[c] ‘bank,’ 57.215) a person who manages or works in a bank
a very hard, translucent, and usually transparent type of quartz
senses.comment: It is also possible that ὕαλος should be interpreted as crystal; see 2.46). In Revelation 21:18 and Revelation 21:21 the emphasis is upon the transparency of the glass.

senses.subdomain: Precious and Semiprecious Stones and Substances
senses.def: a very hard, translucent, and usually transparent type of quartz
senses.comment: The equivalent of ‘crystal’ is often a descriptive phrase such as ‘a brilliant stone’ or ‘a shining stone’ or ‘a glass-like stone.’ In developing a satisfactory term for crystal, it is important to avoid possible confusion with diamond.|Some scholars, however, interpret ὕαλος in Revelation 21:21 as ‘glass’ (see 6.222).

senses.def: to hire a person to act in a particular way, often involving dishonest activities
a small fire which was carried about for the sake of its light and which had some type of protection from wind and weather
senses.comment: Though φανός in earlier Greek meant a torch, by NT times it appears to have been used primarily to identify a type of lamp used outdoors.

senses.def: pertaining to love or affection for those closely related to one, particularly members of one’s immediate family or in-group
a hole, typically occupied by an animal as a den or lair
senses.comment: In most languages it is important to make a distinction between φωλεός as in Luke 9:58 and ὀπή ‘hole’ (1.53), for φωλεός is normally some type of hole serving as a typical habitation or place of escape for an animal, while ὀπή in Hebrews 11:38 would not be a place of normal habitation.

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to have a strong feeling of displeasure and antagonism as the result of some real or supposed wrong
senses.comment: In a number of languages expressions for ‘anger’ are highly idiomatic, for example, ‘his abdomen burned against,’ ‘to be bitter toward,’ or ‘to become red against.’

senses.def: to count up or calculate a total
senses.comment: This process of ‘adding up the number of the beast’ involved calculating the total based upon the numerical values of each of the letters of the name. For another interpretation of ψηφίζω in Revelation 13:18, see 32.15.

senses.def: to come to understand the meaning of something by figuring it out
senses.comment: The third person imperative form ψηφισάτω in Revelation 13:18 is extremely difficult to render in some languages, and even in English the expression ‘let him understand’ is quite misleading, since it might imply permission rather than polite command. In some languages the equivalent of this third person imperative is an expression such as ‘should understand’ or ‘ought to be able to understand.’ For another interpretation of ψηφίζω in Revelation 13:18, see 60.4.
